The New Plan, Zone by Zone

The Village Green (social hub 1). The big open lawn between the swing sycamore and the path becomes an actual town common: fire pit at its heart, well and community board at its edges, and a ring of mismatched seating (log rounds, stools, your metal chairs dressed with throws) arranged mid-gathering around the fire. This is where the witches' social life shows: a meeting interrupted, mugs left on stumps, the Fall Moon Gathering banner strung overhead from the swing sycamore to a lantern post. The macrame swings stay and get dressed witchy: woven swings hanging in a tree next to a village green is exactly what a witch neighborhood would build, and kids can actually use them.

The Inn Terrace (social hub 2). Your elevated patio went unused last year, and it's the best stage in the yard: raised, framed by the two brick wings, reached by steps, visible from the whole lawn. It becomes the Crooked Kettle Inn's terrace: the long feast table set mid-meal (pewter-look plates, bread, candles, chairs pushed back as if everyone just stepped away), lantern strings overhead, your jar fountain dressed as the Inn's spring with a soft glow and mist curling out of its mouth. The house's windows above it get the amber glow and a passing silhouette, so the Inn is visibly occupied. Trick-or-treaters climb the steps to the front door through the middle of an interrupted witch banquet.

The Physic Garden. The berm where the apothecary lived last year is already a witch's herb garden: real perennials dying back photogenically every October, plus your obelisk trellises. Label the plants (Wolfsbane, Widow's Breath, Mandrake: crop failed again), perch a crow on an obelisk, and let the apothecary house sit at the berm's lawn edge with the potion tower and herb arch, so the shop and its growing plot read as one property.

The Allotments. The raised beds by the patio steps become community garden plots, one small painted stake per named witch, each plot dressed to its owner: tiny brooms in the Broom Wright's, bones sprouting in the Sexton's. Cheap, funny, and it puts the cast list in a second place.

The West End. The unused strip left of the driveway is now the quiet side of the village: Shady Willow Cemetery expanded with the Sexton's corner, the distant cottage silhouette at its far end against the garage backdrop, and ground fog rolling. Your rusty burn barrel is already there and is now the Sexton's burn barrel (a faint amber flicker inside it at night). Bristle & Twig and the broom parking sit at the driveway's lawn edge, and your existing lighted metal arch at the corner garden becomes the Tradesman's Gate: the second entrance, dressed with a small sign, so the village has a front door and a back door like any real place. And your squash and pumpkin vines are the best possible news: by October the Tradesman's Gate is a living tunnel of pumpkin vine, which no amount of foam could fake. Leave every arch the vines are climbing exactly where it is; the plan bends around living plants, not the other way round.

The High Street. Coven Market and the seamstress cottage move to the east side facing the green, with the bakery across the path so its serving window faces arriving visitors, and the Diviner's tower stands between the green and the patio steps where its violet doorway is visible from the whole street. The lychgate spans the paver path at the sidewalk, with the fingerpost beside it. One path in, everything radiating off the green, and the patio glowing above it all.

Drag anything you disagree with, copy the layout, and paste it back. Once the bones are approved, the next pass adds the lived-in dressing layer to every zone.

The Residents of Coven Hollow

Hobbiton's rule, which you already follow: every structure belongs to someone with a trade. Season two's theme: give every resident a name, show each mid-task, and keep everything to the village standards: early Victorian look and technology, roughly 3/4 scale, finished on all four sides for the people who wander through.

Current residents YEAR ONE

The Apothecary

Stump house with the moss cap and lit oval window
  • Already there: APOTHECARY sign, herb-drying arch, potion shelf tower, crow on the roof, birdbath, black cat, and the rain boots by the door (exactly the detail set dressers get paid for).
  • Add a work table mid-grind: mortar and pestle, open recipe book, spilled lavender.
  • One bubbling jar (aquarium air pump + colored water) on the shelf tower.
  • A hidden blacklight so a few tonic-water potions glow at dusk while everything else stays warm.
  • A note pinned to the door: “Out gathering nightshade. Back by moonrise.”

Coven Market

The pig's shop. Greengrocer of the strange.
  • Already there: pig mascot roof sign, bunting, pentagram door, folk-painted produce table, birdcages, lantern, and real branding (Salem & Co. Spellgrain Supply, Black Cauldron Milling). You invented supply chains for a yard display. Respect.
  • Name the pig, and put the name on a proprietor plaque. Or let trick-or-treaters vote on a ballot; announce the winner on the community board next year.
  • Chalkboard prices in witch currency: “Dragon eggs, 3 newt eyes each. Screaming beets, ask first.”
  • The chimneys are begging for smoke: a small fog machine ducted up one, on a puff timer.
  • A moving silhouette behind the window (rotating shadow spinner). The shop looks staffed after dark.

The Seamstress

Stone cottage, black swoop roof, diamond window
  • Already there: canvas awning, lantern, the clothesline of black garments, the trunk of hats and cloaks, and the scarecrow family. Free story upgrade: the scarecrows are her mannequins, modeling this season's line. A small sign makes it canon.
  • Dress form wearing a half-finished gown, pins in, measuring tape draped.
  • Sold tags on hats and cloaks bearing customer witches' names (ties into the Owl Post mailboxes).
  • A clip fan hidden low so the laundry flutters.
  • Warm light + slow silhouette behind that diamond stained-glass window. It will glow like a jewel.

Cauldron Fire Pit & Wishing Well

The commons
  • Already there: three cauldrons on the bone-and-branch fire bed, skulls, the witch legs kicking out of one pot, and the wooden well.
  • Make one cauldron stir itself: low-RPM rotisserie motor turning a gnarled dowel. Slow is spookier than fast.
  • Mist maker in one pot, ember glow under the fire bed, green glow in a third.
  • Well upgrade: cool light down inside + a pond mist maker, so it breathes. Sign: “Wishes granted as-is. No warranty.” Scatter pennies to start the collection.

Civic Coven Hollow

Community board, broom parking, ordinances
  • Already there: the Coven Hollow sign, community board (lost cat, wanted toad, Fall Moon Gathering, the raven-caging ordinance), broom hitching rail, hat rack. Connective tissue most yard displays never think of.
  • Season two posters: rotate the flyers so return visitors notice the year changed. A construction notice: “Pardon our dust: new bakery coming to the Hollow.”
  • Add a one-page village newspaper to the board: the Coven Hollow Courier.
  • One broom at the rail gets a parking boot and a citation. Per Hollow ordinance, naturally.

Shady Willow Cemetery

Quietest neighborhood in the Hollow
  • Already there: the lettered sign, black picket fence, chains, mossy pillar.
  • Add foam headstones with resident humor: “She told you she was cursed,” “Allergic to holy water,” “Fine. You stir it then.”
  • One fresh dig with a shovel standing in it (see the Sexton below).
  • This is the ground-fog zone: fog machine through a cooler of ice so it hugs the grass.

Proposed new residents YEAR TWO

The Baker

Cackle Crust Bakery
  • A four-sided, walk-around early Victorian shop at 3/4 scale, and the one building in the village you can see into: an open serving window where a real person stands inside at the counter to sell bread and hand out treats, plus a nine-pane display window stacked with goods and a display board of loaves out front.
  • The story writes itself: you already invented Black Cauldron Milling. The bakery is who buys the flour; branded sacks stack by the staff door.
  • Brick chimney with clay pots and a lazy fog-machine smoke drift. When unstaffed, the serving space reads as a baker thirty seconds gone: apron on its hook, scale mid-weigh, open ledger.

The Postmistress

Owl Post. Night delivery only.
  • A kiosk with twelve pigeonhole mailboxes, one per named witch: the village's cast list in one place.
  • The brass letter slot is real. Kids post letters to the residents all October; wax-sealed replies appear on the community board next year.
  • Now the raven ordinance has a reason: the ravens carry the mail. “Do not cage the ravens” is labor law.

The Broom Wright

Bristle & Twig. Sales, service, crash recovery.
  • A mono-pitch trade workshop with plank doors thrown open: workbench, vise, half-bound broom, shavings, and a giant hanging broom as its Victorian trade sign.
  • Your existing parking rail becomes the customer lot (one broom booted, with citation); your grass sheaves become the bristle stock.
  • The photo magnet: a crashed broom lodged in a tree, tagged “RECOVERY REQUESTED, awaiting ladder.”

The Diviner

Fortunes, star charts, weather hexes
  • A slim hexagonal tower in midnight blue with gold stars, a moon dial, a brass telescope through a shutter, and a crescent finial. Different palette on purpose: her house is different because she is.
  • Velvet-curtained doorway glowing violet: the village's one sanctioned exception to the flame-light rule.
  • Her weather forecast pins to the community board: “Tonight: full dark, 100% chance of spirits.”

The Sexton

Shady Willow Cemetery staff of one
  • Sexton is the proper Victorian word for the gravedigger-groundskeeper, and somebody digs. A small open-front tool shed at the cemetery edge: shovels hung, lantern lit, wheelbarrow parked somewhere new each night.
  • The fresh dig: soil mound, standing shovel, gloves on a headstone, half-eaten lunch on a crate. He'll be back.

Unseen Neighbors

Implied population
  • Tiny arched doors at the base of the big tree with doormats, micro lit portholes, and their own tiny scarlet mailboxes.
  • A half-scale black cottage silhouette with one warm lit window in the darkest corner. Forced perspective; the Hollow continues into the dark.
  • Owl Post mailboxes for witches who have no house at all. Absence with a name is free immersion.

Immersion Layers

Hobbiton feels inhabited because of smoke, laundry, and half-finished chores: evidence of life. You have the daytime version nailed. Season two's biggest opportunity is the night shift: light, sound, and motion, layered in that order, all of it reading early Victorian (flame-warm, hand-made, nothing visibly newer than about 1845). Build Sheets. Year Two. Full construction set.

Village standards on every build: early Victorian look and technology (flame-warm light, gilt serif signage, iron and brass, nothing visibly newer than about 1845), roughly 3/4 scale with functional parts near full size, four finished sides on anything visitors walk around, pin-hinge collapse where it earns its hardware, and anchoring rated past your canyon gusts. Each sheet ends with a photoreal concept prompt: paste it into image generation in the regular Claude chat to preview the finished build. Looking for the fingerpost? It shares Sheet 4 with the lychgate. The far cottage shares Sheet 7 with the tiny doors. Sheets 8–11 cover the new zones from the map. The Chimney Rule (village law): every chimney on every build ships smoke-ready, meaning a hollow core sized for 4″ duct, clear ground space at its base for a fog machine in a weather box, a cord path to the nearest power zone, and a restricted 2–3″ exit at the top. A chimney that cannot breathe does not get built.
Sheet 1 · Cackle Crust Bakery (rev. C: four-sided, walk-in, collapsible)
Generated concept, approved direction for this build.
Early Victorian gable-front shop, ~3/4 scale · footprint 72″ × 60″ · walls 66″, ridge 84″, chimney pots to ~112″ · a real person stands inside to sell · folds flat on hinges · rated for canyon gusts · ~$180–260 · three weekends

An 1840s village bakery at the Hollow's scale: about three-quarters of full size, finished on all four sides for the people who wander through, and open where every other building is shut. The front gable carries a Victorian shopfront: a serving window where you (or whoever plays baker that night) stand inside at a real counter to sell bread and hand out treats, and a small-paned display window stacked with goods, with a display board of loaves out front. The whole building is four hinged wall panels plus a folding roof: it goes up in twenty minutes, pins together rigid, stakes to the ground against canyon wind, and stores as a flat stack in November.

The 3/4-scale cheat sheet

Theme parks shrink buildings the same way: the dressing shrinks, the functional parts don't. Anything a human touches stays near full size; anything the eye measures goes to 3/4. That's what makes a small building read as charming instead of wrong.

Shrinks to 3/4Stays functional (near full size)
Wall heights, roof pitch mass, clapboard exposure (4.5″), shingle exposure, window pane size, sign lettering, door and trim proportionsServing counter at 34″ (a real seller's height), door clear opening 26″ × 62″ (adults duck slightly, which feels like entering a cottage), interior headroom 78″+ at the ridge line

Front elevation

Front elevation, rev. C. Gable-front means full standing height right at the counter, so the seller works comfortably at the serving window. Left bay: raised sash, lit interior, apron on its hook. Right bay: nine-pane display window over a paneled stallriser, display board of loaves in front. A 5'6″ figure shown for the 3/4-scale effect.

Plan view & fold scheme

Plan and fold scheme. Two corners get ordinary fixed hinges; the two diagonal corners get loose-pin hinges (3 per corner). Pins in: a rigid closed box. Pins out: two L-pairs that fold flat. This becomes the standard system for every four-sided build in the Hollow.

Wind plan (canyon gusts)

Design target: your ~17 mph canyon winds with margin to roughly 30 mph gusts. A closed four-sided box is already the strongest shape in this village; wind pushes on about 35 sq ft of wall and meets a staked, pinned ring of panels instead of a flat sail. The load on the worst wall in a 30 mph gust is on the order of 80 lb, and the anchoring below covers that several times over.

  • Corners pinned full height: 3 hinges per corner (top, middle, bottom) so the box acts as one ring, not four flaps.
  • Four 18″ rebar stakes, one through each corner base plate, driven at a slight inward lean.
  • Roof positively attached: 8 hook-and-eyes (2 per roof edge) latching roof frame to wall plates. Roof lift is the only real failure mode; gravity is not a fastener.
  • Two 30 lb sandbags inside against the side walls (invisible from outside, they double as prop weights).
  • Optional for exposed spots: a ratchet strap over the ridge to two spiral ground anchors, hidden under the ridge cap trim.

The serving space (where you stand)

Inside is a real workspace: standing room at the counter (full height, thanks to the gable front), candy and bread within reach, and set dressing that reads as a baker who just stepped into the back. When no one is staffing it, the space still tells the story:

  • The apron on its hook just inside the opening, strings dangling.
  • A rolling pin set down mid-task with flour dust around it (flour sealed under matte spray).
  • A brass balance scale mid-weigh, one pan holding a paper-wrapped loaf tied with twine.
  • An open ledger with a dip pen across it. One visible entry: “Apothecary. 2 soul cakes. UNPAID.”
  • A brass counter bell and a card: “Ring bell. Or don't. She hears everything anyway.”
  • Interior shelves of foam loaves with one gap where something just sold. A shelf at hip height inside holds the real candy stock, out of sight.

Panel framing

Panel framing. Every panel is a 2x2 frame with foam board skin, light enough for one person to carry, joined at the corners by hinges. The 3/4-scale roof pitch comes from the 18″ rise over the 36″ half-span.

Assembly order

  1. Build six panels flat: two gable panels (front and back), two side walls, two roof panels. 2x2 frames, gussets at every joint, blocking where the drawing shows it.
  2. Skin, carve, paint flat. Foam board on (adhesive + washer screws), clapboard scored with a ballpoint pen, timber paint (dark base, gray dry-brush, cream on the raised grain, dark wash in the scores). Painting flat on sawhorses beats painting standing up in every way.
  3. Shopfront joinery on the front panel: pilasters built out 1″ proud with molding caps, stallriser panels in dark green, cornice, and the gable sign hand-lettered in gilt over guide lines.
  4. Serving window: fixed raised sash with lattice muntins, counter bolted to its blocking at 34″.
  5. Display window: clear plastic behind a nine-pane muntin grid, two shallow shelves behind it, stocked. Flicker bulb low inside.
  6. Staff door hung on the back panel, 26″ clear, painted as a paneled Victorian door.
  7. Hinge the box: stand panels in place, fixed hinges at two corners, loose-pin hinges at the two diagonal corners, 3 per corner. Check the box squares up, then number every hinge leaf with a paint pen for next-year assembly.
  8. Roof: piano hinge at the ridge joins the two panels; foam shingles with 3/4-scale exposure; hook-and-eyes latch it to the wall plates. Ridge cap trim hides the hinge (and the optional strap).
  9. Chimney on the right side wall: form tube on its mast, brick-scored skin, terracotta pots, smoke gap in the cap.
  10. Smoke rig: fog machine in a vented weather box at the chimney base, duct up, fan under the cap, one cycle timer: ten seconds of puff, ninety of rest.
  11. Anchor: four rebar stakes through the corner plates, sandbags inside, hook-and-eyes latched. Shake test at the ridge.
  12. Dress the set: serving space per the list, display board on trestles, Black Cauldron Milling sacks by the staff door, A-frame chalkboard by the path (“Soul cakes 2d. Hot cross buns, blessing included. Day-old spells half off.”), cinnamon broom behind the sacks, interior amber strip on, lantern lit.
Village standards set by this sheet, for every build from here on: roughly 3/4 scale with functional parts kept near full size; four finished sides on anything visitors walk around; the pin-hinge panel system for collapse; corner stakes + positive roof attachment + interior ballast for canyon wind; and early Victorian everywhere: flame-warm light only, hand-painted gilt serif signage, iron and brass hardware, wood, wicker, paper, and cloth containers, prices in pence, and every cord and machine hidden inside a build or weather box. Nothing invented after about 1845 in sight.

Sheet 2 · The Owl Post
Generated concept, approved direction for this build.
Early Victorian post office kiosk, ~3/4 scale · footprint 30″ × 30″ · walls 56″, ridge 78″ · 12 named mailboxes · working letter slot · one weekend · ~$60–100 · night delivery only

The smallest build in the village and the one that does the most narrative work: a wall of pigeonhole mailboxes puts every witch's name in one place, so every sold tag, citation, and ledger entry elsewhere in the Hollow suddenly connects to a resident. Early Victorian post office details throughout: dark green paneling, gilt lettering, brass fittings, and a raven on the ridge with an envelope, since in this village the ravens carry the mail (which is why the ordinance forbids caging them; they're the workforce). Small enough that it doesn't need the fold system: it moves whole, the roof lifts off, and it stores standing up.

Front elevation

Front elevation. The gilt sign, the pigeonhole wall with a name under every box, a brass posting slot that actually works, and the raven postman on the ridge. One cubby glows amber from behind: somebody's got mail.

Side section, access & the pillar box accessory

Side section. The rear panel swings open for restocking and letter collection. The pillar box is a bonus evening build from a leftover form tube: the classic scarlet mail pillar with the Hollow's cipher where the crown's would be. Place it along the path away from the kiosk so the mail system feels like infrastructure.

The mailbox names (the cast list)

Twelve boxes. Eight belong to residents visitors can find, four belong to witches who exist only as names, which is exactly the kind of loose thread that makes a village feel bigger than its yard. Suggested layout until you christen them properly:

The letter slot game

  • The brass slot is real: kids post letters to the residents all October.
  • A small placard: “Letters to the residents of Coven Hollow. Replies delivered by raven before next All Hallows.”
  • Next year, a few replies (tea-stained, wax-sealed, signed by the witches) get pinned to the community board. The neighborhood kids who wrote will lose their minds.
  • Collection is just opening the rear panel and emptying the bin.

Assembly order

  1. Frame the box: four 56″ corner posts, rails top and bottom on all four sides, gussets at the joints. At this size the frame is rigid without mid studs.
  2. Roof as a lift-off lid: a shallow 2x2 pyramid/gable frame skinned in foam, sitting over the wall tops on locating blocks, hooked down with 4 hook-and-eyes. No piano hinge needed at this scale.
  3. Skin, carve, paint flat before assembly where you can: clapboard scoring, timber paint, dark green sign field and stallriser, gilt lettering over guide lines.
  4. Cubby grid: egg-crate slotted strips glued into a 3 × 4 grid, 8″ deep, backed with a foam panel. Or mount a thrifted cubby unit and trim foam around it, which is faster and usually looks better.
  5. Slot and bin: cut the slot through wall and ledge, mount the brass plate, set the bin below inside.
  6. Rear access panel on 2 hinges with a hook latch.
  7. Perch and raven: dowel socket at the ridge; the raven lifts out for storage.
  8. Anchor and dress: 4 corner stakes, sandbag inside, lantern lit, cubbies stocked with letter bundles, one backlit, parcels stacked beside, hours placard: “Night delivery only. Closed during full moons (staff molting).”

Sheet 3 · Bristle & Twig, Broom Wrights
Generated concept, approved direction for this build.
Early Victorian trade workshop, ~3/4 scale · footprint 60″ × 48″ · front wall 66″, mono-pitch roof falling to 50″ · doors stand open, interior on display · pin-hinge collapsible · one to two weekends · ~$100–150 · brooms made, mended & recovered from trees

The workshop that explains your existing broom parking rail: somebody has to service all those brooms. Where the bakery is a shop, this is a trade building, so it gets a workshop's shape: a mono-pitch roof sloping from a tall front to a low back, plank double doors thrown open all evening, and the workbench in plain view with a broom half-bound in the vise. Victorian trade shops hung oversized symbols of their craft over the street (a giant boot, a giant key), so Bristle & Twig hangs a giant broom. Your existing bound grass sheaves finally get their backstory: they're the raw bristle stock, stacked against the wall.

Front elevation

Front elevation. Doors pinned open against the wall, lantern-lit interior on display: tool wall, twine spools, and the workbench with a broom half-bound in the vise, shavings on the floor. The giant broom trade sign hangs over the path; the stock rack sells finished brooms in pence.

Plan & side section

Plan and section. The mono-pitch roof is one panel, making this the easiest collapse in the village. Doors fold flat against the wall and hook there; in a serious wind warning, lift them off their pin hinges entirely and lay them inside.

Set dressing & gags

  • The bench mid-task: a broom clamped in the vise with binding twine still wrapped around it and hanging loose. Real wood shavings on the floor, free from any woodshop.
  • Stock rack outside: four to six finished brooms, paper tags in pence (“4d”, “6d, ash handle”), one tagged SOLD in a witch's name once the cast is christened.
  • The customer lot: your existing parking rail gets a “BRISTLE & TWIG CUSTOMERS ONLY” placard, one broom wears a boot with a citation tied on (“Per Hollow ordinance 7: overnight roosting”).
  • The tow job: a crashed broom wedged in a nearby tree or hedge, tagged “RECOVERY REQUESTED, awaiting ladder.” The most photographed square foot in the yard, guaranteed.
  • The fitting post: a marked measuring post by the door: “Broom fitting: stand here.” Height marks labeled “First broom,” “Learner,” “Licensed,” “Show-off.” Kids measure themselves all night and it costs you one post and a paint pen.
  • Repair queue: three or four battered brooms leaning by the door with paper claim tickets: “bent in a hex,” “cat damage,” “pulls left.”

Cut list

MaterialCutQtyUsed for
2x2 x 8'front/back wall frames (66″ and 50″ studs), side frames, blocking~12 sticksfour wall panels
2x2 x 8'rails + rungs for one ~52″ × 62″ panel3 sticksroof panel
1″ foam board 4'x8'trimmed on frames6wall skins, roof skin, sign build-out, trim

1x10 boardone @ 56″1workbench top (thrifted small bench beats building one)
Dowels/branchesgathered crooked handles6+broom stock; harvest and dry them now, bind in September
Ply/foam scrapgiant broom silhouette ~36″1hanging trade sign
4″ black duct + elbow~40″1optional stove pipe on the back wall
Hinge hardware6 loose-pin, 6 fixed, 8 hook-and-eyes, 2 pair door pin hinges, 2 cabin hooks—corners, roof, doors
18″ rebar stakes—4corner anchors

Assembly order

  1. Four wall panels flat: front (66″) with the 40″ × 52″ opening framed, back (50″), two trapezoid sides. Gussets everywhere.
  2. Skin, carve, paint flat: clapboard scoring and the timber paint recipe from Sheet 1; dark green for doors and sign field.
  3. Doors: two plank leaves with Z-bracing, hung on pin hinges so they lift off; cabin hooks hold them open against the wall.
  4. Pin-hinge the box (Sheet 1 system: two fixed corners, two loose-pin corners, three hinges each, leaves numbered with a paint pen).
  5. Roof panel on: one mono-pitch panel, hook-and-eyes to both wall plates. Fascia board across the tall front hides the panel edge.
  6. Sign work: gilt letter the fascia sign over guide lines; cut, paint, and hang the giant broom from its bracket with two eye bolts (it should swing a little; that's the charm).
  7. Interior: bench against the back wall, vise, tool silhouettes (real rusty tools from the antique list, or foam cutouts painted black), twine spool shelf, hanging lantern with a flame bulb, shavings scattered.
  8. Anchor and dress: four corner stakes, sandbag inside, stock rack planted outside, fitting post, repair queue, boot and citation on the parking rail, crashed broom in the tree.

Sheet 4 · The Lychgate & Fingerpost
Generated concept, approved direction for this build.
Village entrance, early Victorian lychgate style · 48″ opening, posts 78″, roof peak ~92″ · posts drop into ground sleeves (lift out to store) · one weekend · ~$50–80

English villages of this era marked their thresholds with lychgates: a small roofed gate you pass beneath. That's exactly the job here. Crossing under a roof, even a tiny one, tells visitors the rules changed on the other side. The sign facing the street says where they've arrived; the sign on the back, which they only see leaving, says what they're returning to. The fingerpost stands just inside, pointing the way to every resident.

Elevation

The lychgate and fingerpost. Back of the hanging sign reads “NOW RETURNING TO THE MORTAL WORLD. MIND THE GAP BETWEEN REALITIES.” The fingerpost's arrows point at the real buildings, so the joke also works as wayfinding.

Build notes

PartHow
PostsTwo 4x4s (or doubled 2x4s) @ 78″, wrapped in spray-foam bark ridges carved back with a knife, painted, moss pressed into the wet paint. They drop into buried pipe sleeves (1 ft of 2″ PVC set in the ground), which is the whole collapse system: lift out, cap the sleeves, mow over them all year.
Beam & roofA found gnarled branch or a 2x6 cut wavy, lag-bolted across the posts. The lychgate roof is a small 2x2 gable frame skinned in foam shingles, ~30″ deep, screwed to the beam. Moss the edges.
SignsHanging sign on two eye bolts so it swings: dark green field, gilt serif both faces. Fingerpost arrows: 1x6 scraps cut to points, lettered with the paint pen, mounted at alternating angles. A finial bead on top.
LightOne lantern with a flame bulb hung from the beam. The gate should be the brightest point on the sidewalk line so it pulls people in.
WindThe sleeves do the work: a post in a ground sleeve laughs at 30 mph. The roof is small enough to shrug gusts; use three screws per side anyway.

Sheet 5 · The Diviner's Tower
Generated concept, approved direction for this build.
Hexagonal observatory tower, ~3/4 scale · 36″ across flats · walls 66″, cone peak ~96″ · accordion-fold collapse · two weekends · ~$110–160 · fortunes, star charts & weather hexes

Every building so far is a tradesman's: timber, green paint, gilt. The Diviner is not a tradesman, and her house says so. A slim six-sided tower in midnight blue scattered with gold stars, a moon dial on the wall, a brass telescope poking through a shutter at the sky, and a curtained doorway lit from within. Early Victorians were mad for astronomy (backyard observatories were a genuine craze), so the tower reads period AND otherworldly. She earns the village's one exception to the flame-light rule: her doorway glows a slow violet, because scrying is in progress, and one cool light in a warm village reads as magic.

Elevation & fold plan

Elevation and fold plan. Midnight blue with gold stars against a village of timber grays: her house is different because she is. The doorway's violet glow is the Hollow's single sanctioned exception to the flame-light rule.

Build notes

PartHow
FacetsSix 21″ × 66″ foam-on-2x2 panels, corner-hinged at 120°: four fixed corners, two loose-pin corners opposite each other. Pins out, it splits into two shells that accordion flat. The hex needs no interior frame; the geometry is its own bracing.
Cone roofSix foam triangles taped and glued over a light 2x2 spider, or one 4x8 sheet scored, rolled, and seamed. Painted near-black blue with sparse gold stars. Crescent finial from doubled foam board on a dowel. Hook-and-eyes to the wall plates like every roof in the village.
PaintMidnight blue base, near-black blue on alternating facets for depth, gold paint-pen stars sparse at the bottom and denser toward the cone (the sky gets thicker as you go up). Moon dial: gold rings and a crescent on a dark disc.
Telescope3″ PVC + a 2″ coupler “eyepiece,” brass spray paint, through a shuttered opening, aimed somewhere above the neighbors' roofline.
DoorwayArched opening with real curtain fabric (thrifted velvet), a slow color-shifting LED puck inside set to drift between violet and deep blue. A small table silhouette behind the curtain gap: crystal ball (glass fishing float from the grail list) catching the glow.
WindHexagons are wind's least favorite shape: no flat face square to the gust. Four stakes through alternating facet plates, one sandbag inside. Done.
Paper propsHer forecast pinned to the community board, refreshed weekly in October: “Tonight: full dark, waxing dread, 100% chance of spirits. Bring a coat.”

Sheet 6 · The Sexton's Corner
Generated concept, approved direction for this build.
Shady Willow Cemetery staff quarters · lean-to shed 40″ × 24″, front 54″ · plus a headstone kit and the fresh dig · scattered evenings · ~$60–90 · inquiries discouraged

Victorian graveyards had a sexton: the man who kept the grounds, rang the bell, and dug. Your Shady Willow Cemetery already has the fence, the sign, and the chains; what it's missing is the evidence of staff. A small lean-to tool shed, a scatter of properly carved headstones, and one fresh dig with the shovel still standing in it turns the corner from decoration into a workplace where somebody just knocked off for supper.

Shed & headstone kit

The sexton's shed (open-front lean-to, tools hung and lantern lit) plus the headstone kit: three silhouettes to cut in multiples. Lean two extra blanks against the shed, uncarved: business is steady.

Build notes

PartHow
ShedSheet 3 shrunk: 40″ × 24″, front 54″ to back 42″, one roof panel, open front bay (no doors), pin-hinge corners, 4 stakes. One evening of framing, one of skin and paint.
Headstones2″ XPS foam. Cut silhouettes with a hot wire or knife, letter with a hot knife or ballpoint-pressed grooves, charcoal wash, two gray dry-brush passes, moss in the crevices and along one shoulder (weather hits one side; keep the moss consistent to your yard's north). Each stone rides an 18″ wood stake glued into a slot in its base.
Epitaph bank“She told you she was cursed.” “Fine. You stir it then.” “Allergic to holy water.” “Out of office. Permanently.” “Beloved. Feared. Both.” One stone lettered only “RESERVED,” freshly planted at the dig.
The digA low soil mound (bagged topsoil over a tarp saves the lawn), shovel standing in it, work gloves on the nearest headstone, a lunch pail and half-eaten bread on an overturned crate. He'll be back.
FogThis corner gets the ground fog: fog machine through an ice chiller (cooler + dryer hose + ice) hidden behind the fence line, timer-puffed. Cold fog crawls; warm fog leaves. Chill it.
SoundQuietest audio zone in the village: wind, a slow creak, one distant owl. No music here. Silence is the cemetery's instrument.

Sheet 7 · Tiny Doors & the Distant Cottage
Generated concept, approved direction for this build.
The implied population · tiny doors 10″ × 14″ at tree bases · cottage silhouette 40″ × 48″ in the darkest corner · scattered evenings · ~$30–50 · residents you never meet

The cheapest square feet in the whole village, and among the most effective. Tiny doors at the bases of real trees imply residents at a whole other scale, living their own lives underfoot. The distant cottage is a flat black silhouette with one warm lit window, parked in the darkest corner of the yard: from the sidewalk it reads as another street of the Hollow trailing off into the dark. Both work by the same rule: the imagination finishes whatever the light starts.

Details

The tiny door gets real hardware details (strap hinges, a brass bead knob, a GO AWAY mat, its own scarlet mailbox on a twig post). The cottage is matte black plywood or foam with one warm window; darkness does the rest of the construction for free.

Build notes

PartHow
Tiny doors (make 2–3)Scrap 1x material or doubled foam board, arched, plank-scored, with strap hinges cut from black foam and a bead or drawer-pull knob. Porthole window backed with amber film and a micro fairy light (coin battery with timer, swapped weekly). Strap to the tree with a black bungee behind ivy, or lean-stake it; never screw into the tree.
DressingDoormat from a sample scrap lettered in paint pen. A twig-post mailbox, scarlet like the pillar box: the Owl Post delivers at every scale. Optional milk-bottle-cap sized bottles by the door on delivery day.
CottageOne sheet of 1/2″ ply or foam board cut as a gabled silhouette with a chimney, painted the flattest black available. The window opening gets amber film and a flicker bulb in a weatherproof box behind. Two stakes and a kickstand, plus one sandbag: it's a flat, so treat it like a sail and tuck it into the wind shadow of the fence or shrubs.
PlacementThe whole trick is placement: darkest corner, partially masked by real foliage, window angled toward the sidewalk sightline. If a visitor can see its edges, move it deeper. The moment it reads clearly, it stops working.
Scale noteThe cottage is roughly half scale, and that's on purpose. Smaller than the 3/4-scale village implies it's far away: forced perspective doing the work of thirty feet of yard you don't have.

8. The Inn Terrace & Feast Table ~$80–140 · mostly dressing · the showpiece
Your existing patio, furniture rearranged or cleared · the one scene visitors will describe to their friends

The patio becomes the terrace of the Crooked Kettle Inn, and its centerpiece is a feast interrupted. The story: the Fall Moon Gathering banquet was in progress, something called the whole coven away mid-course, and visitors arrive minutes later.

PartHow
The tableAny long table (folding banquet table works) skirted in dark fabric with a burlap or lace runner. Ten mismatched chairs and stools, several pushed back at angles, one tipped fully over. Nothing says “left in a hurry” like a fallen chair no one righted.
The mealPewter-look plates (thrifted, or spray-painted charger plates), goblets, a foam roast centerpiece, bread, grapes, candlesticks with flame bulbs, half-poured pitcher. Two or three plates half-eaten (foam props), napkins dropped. One hat left on a chair back.
OverheadLantern strings zig-zagged between the two brick wings (anchor to eaves), flame-warm only. Low enough to glow on the table.
The springYour jar fountain, dressed: soft amber puck light inside the mouth, pond mist maker in the basin, moss around the rim. Sign: “The Kettle Spring. Waters of questionable origin.”
The Inn itselfHanging sign near the front door (“THE CROOKED KETTLE INN · no vacancies. ever.”), amber window film + a shadow-spinner silhouette in one window above the terrace, boots by the door, a stack of tiny guest trunks.
FunctionCandy handoff happens here or at the bakery window: kids walk up the steps through the banquet to reach the door. Keep the walking lane down one side of the table clear and lit.

9. The Village Green ~$40–80 · arrangement, not construction · social hub 1
A composed circle on the open lawn: fire pit at the heart, well and board at the edges, seating mid-gathering
PartHow
The circleRoughly 16 ft across, centered between the swing sycamore and the paver path. Mow the lawn one notch shorter inside the circle the week before; the ground itself will read as a village common.
The heartThe cauldron fire pit (with the Rig B stirrer, ember bed, and mist from the Upgrades tab) sits at center.
The ringEight to ten mismatched seats facing the fire: log rounds, stools, crates, your metal chairs draped in dark throws. On them: left-behind mugs, a knitting project mid-row, an open book face down, a lantern, a shawl. A gathering paused, not a display arranged.
The lantern postOne 8' post (pipe-sleeved like the lychgate) at the circle's edge, crossarm on top: banner line runs from it to the swing sycamore. Banner: “FALL MOON GATHERING · ALL HALLOWS · BRING A DISH & A DREAD.”
EdgesWell and community board stand at the circle's rim (the board freshly posted per the Upgrades tab), Owl Post just off it on the path side. The swings in the sycamore overhang the green: woven swings by a common is exactly what witches would build, and kids can use them.
Sound & lightBubbling and low chatter loop near the fire, path lanterns around the rim, the hat lanterns floating in the sycamore above.

10. The Physic Garden & The Allotments ~$30–50 · scattered evenings · your real plants do the heavy lifting
The berm (the apothecary's old site) and the raised beds, recruited as working witch agriculture
PartHow
The Physic GardenYour berm perennials, dying back photogenically every October, get labeled as the apothecary's crop: aged stakes reading Wolfsbane, Widow's Breath, Feverfew (true), Mandrake (crop failed. again.), Do Not Water After Midnight. Tea-stained tags on copper wire. The obelisk trellises get a crow perched on one and a tiny warning bell on another.
The shop adjoinsThe apothecary stump house sits at the berm's lawn edge with the potion tower and herb arch, so shop and growing plot read as one property. A harvest basket half-full of cuttings sits abandoned between them, shears still in it.
The AllotmentsEach raised bed section gets a small painted stake with a witch's name and a plot dressed to its owner: tiny brooms sprouting like seedlings in the Broom Wright's plot, foam bones "growing" in rows in the Sexton's, a miniature bubbling pot sunk in the Apothecary's, pumpkins (real, from your vines) in the Baker's. A little hand-painted rules board: “ALLOTMENT RULES: no cursing thy neighbor's crop.”
LightOne amber uplight raking the berm from the lawn side so the obelisks and seed heads silhouette after dark. The garden needs nothing else; dead perennials at night are already perfect.

11. The Tradesman's Gate ~$25–40 · one evening · the vines are doing the real work
Your existing corner light arch, which your squash and pumpkin vines will own by October. Do not move it; dress it.
PartHow
The vinesAlready planted, already climbing. A living pumpkin-vine tunnel is the one thing in this village no foam could fake, so the entire build plan here is: help them along, and get out of the way. Train runners over the crown through summer; come October, any gaps get filled with a few cut vines and real gourds wired in among the true ones.
The signA small hanging board under the crown: “TRADESMAN'S GATE · deliveries, brooms & familiars.” Dark green, gilt serif, both faces.
The lightsYour existing string bulbs on the arch swap to flame-flicker LEDs so the tunnel glows warm through the leaves.
The detailsAn ordinance plaque on the picket fence (“Gate closes at moonset. Latecomers: use the chimney.”), a parked delivery broom leaning inside the arch with a laden basket, and a “WATCH FOR TOADS” sign at ankle height for the kids who read everything.
RoleThis is the village's back door, feeding the West End: through the gate, visitors meet Bristle & Twig, then the cemetery beyond. Front door (lychgate) for the show; Tradesman's Gate for the wanderers.

Upgrade Sheets. The Year-One Builds.

Nothing here replaces what you built. These sheets add the night shift (light, motion, smoke, sound) and the Victorian conformance pass to structures that already work. Three shared rigs power most of it, so the Rig Shop sheet comes first; every structure sheet after it just says which rigs it takes. Standards apply as everywhere: flame-warm light, hidden cords, prices in pence, nothing visibly newer than about 1845 (the Diviner's violet doorway stays the only exception).
The Rig Shop · three builds you'll reuse everywhere
One evening each · the spinner ~$25, the stirrer ~$30, the chiller ~$25 · build once, deploy anywhere

Rig A. The shadow spinner (moving window silhouettes)

A lamp, a slowly turning carousel with two black witch cutouts on its rim, a frosted window. From the street: someone is moving around in there.
PartsNotes
1–3 RPM AC synchronous motor ($8–12)Sold as “mirror ball motor” or “rotating display stand.” Slow is the whole trick; 5+ RPM reads as comedy.
12″ foam-core disc + two 10″ witch cutoutsCutouts glued standing on the rim, facing out, different poses. Matte black.
Clamp lamp + flame-flicker LED18–24″ behind the carousel, at cutout height, aimed at the window.
Frosted window film (or parchment paper)On the inside of the glass so the silhouette reads soft, not sharp.

Deploys at: Coven Market window, the seamstress's diamond window, and eventually the bakery. Build one per window; at ~$25 each, the market and seamstress together are the best fifty dollars in this whole plan.

Rig B. The self-stirring cauldron

The motor and the false surface hide inside the pot; all a visitor sees is a crooked stick slowly circling a bubbling brew on its own.
PartsNotes
BBQ rotisserie motor ($12–18)Slow, strong, made for outdoors, runs all night. Thrift stores are full of them.
Plywood disc cut to sit 2″ below the rimSkinned with carved spray foam, painted; a gloss-varnish center circle reads as liquid.
Gnarled dowel or branch, mounted 2–3″ off-centerOff-center is what makes rotation read as stirring.
Optional pond mist maker + cup of waterRecessed into the lid next to the stirrer.

Rig C. The ground-fog chiller

Warm fog rises and vanishes; chilled fog crawls. The cooler costs nothing if you already own one, and the cemetery earns it most.
U1 · The Apothecary (stump house)
~$40–60 in parts · two evenings · the moss-and-bark work stays exactly as it is
UpgradeHowEst.
Bubbling jarA large clear jar of water tinted green (a drop of glycerin thickens the bubbles), aquarium air pump hidden in the potion tower, airline tubing up through the lid, check valve so water can't back-siphon. Runs silent, mesmerizes children indefinitely.$12
Glowing potionsA small UV flood tucked under a shelf of the potion tower, aimed up. Tonic water potions and a few UV-paint accents glow; keep the zone tight so the rest of the vignette stays flame-warm.$15
Work table mid-grindMortar and pestle with crushed herbs actually in it, an open recipe book (tea-staged pages, hand-written), spilled dried lavender. Ten minutes of staging, disproportionate payoff.$0 + finds
Poison gardenPlant stakes among the real plants by the door: Wolfsbane, Mandrake (crop failed, again), Widow's Breath, Do Not Water After Midnight. Foam-board tags aged with tea, wired to copper stakes.$5
The door note“Out gathering nightshade. Back by moonrise.” Pinned with a thorn. Re-pin a different note occasionally; repeat visitors notice.$0
Oval window silhouetteRig A, small version: the window already glows; a cat-silhouette cutout on a mini carousel behind it means her familiar patrols the sill.$20
U2 · Coven Market
~$60–90 in parts · two evenings · the pig is already perfect, change nothing about the pig
UpgradeHowEst.
Chimney smokeThe bakery's rig, sized down: small fog machine in a vented bin behind the building, ducted up one of the existing chimneys, PC fan at top, cycle timer (10s puff / 90s rest). The market visibly cooking is the single biggest upgrade to the existing village.$45
Window silhouetteRig A behind the market window. Between the smoke and a moving shadow, this shop is unmistakably staffed after dark.$25
Witch pricingChalkboard tags on the produce: “Dragon eggs, 3 newt eyes ea.” “Screaming beets, ask first.” “Watermelons, mortal, 2d.” Mixing mortal pence and witch barter is funnier than either alone.$5
The proprietorA small plaque for the pig: name pending your christening (or a trick-or-treater ballot box on the counter this year, winner announced on the community board next).$3
Brass scale mid-weighFrom the grail list: hanging or balance scale on the produce table, one pan loaded with gourds.find
Victorian sweepFlame bulb in the existing lantern if it isn't already, cords re-routed behind the stallrisers, and the bunting stays because a market gets bunting in any century.$8
U3 · The Seamstress Cottage
~$40–60 in parts · one to two evenings · the diamond window becomes the jewel of the village
UpgradeHowEst.
The diamond windowWarm light behind the colored panes plus Rig A with a single cutout: a seamstress shape that passes with an armful of cloth. Stained glass with a moving shadow behind it will stop traffic.$30
Laundry that fluttersClip fan hidden low behind the hay bale, on the same dusk timer, aimed along the clothesline. Motion you notice without ever seeing why.$15
Dress form vignetteGrail-list dress form wearing a half-finished gown, pins in, measuring tape draped, scissors open on the sill. Until the form turns up, the trunk of cloaks does the job with one gown draped half-out.find
The mannequinsA small sign by the scarecrow family: “This season's line. Modeled nightly.” Your existing scarecrows become her staff retroactively, for the price of one sign.$3
Sold tagsPaper tags on hats and cloaks: SOLD, with witch names once christened. Cross-references the Owl Post mailboxes.$0
U4 · Cauldron Commons & the Wishing Well
~$70–100 in parts · two evenings · your fire pit already has the bones (literally); this adds the life
UpgradeHowEst.
One cauldron stirsRig B in the largest pot. The witch legs stay kicking out of their pot; the third pot gets the green glow. Three pots, three behaviors, one story: brewing in progress.$30
Ember bedAmber flicker string light woven under the branch pile with red cellophane scraps. From the street the fire bed breathes.$12
SteamPond mist maker in a water dish inside the stirring pot (built into Rig B's lid) or the legs pot. Real cool steam, no fog juice, silent.$15
Bubbling audioA small weatherproof speaker under the pots: slow bubbling loop, volume low enough that kids lean in.$15
The well breathesCool-white puck light down the shaft + a mist maker in a hidden water dish on a shelf inside. Sign: “Wishes granted as-is. No warranty.” Scatter two dollars of pennies the first night; the collection grows itself all month.$20
U5 · Civic Hollow (board, rail, cemetery dressing)
~$20 in parts, mostly paper and paint · the cheapest sheet and the one that makes the village feel governed
UpgradeHowEst.
Season two postersRotate the board: this year's Fall Moon Gathering date, a construction notice (“Pardon our dust: Cackle Crust Bakery, opening All Hallows”), the Diviner's weekly forecast, and keep the lost cat up (she's about to become a game).$0
The Coven Hollow CourierOne tea-stained page, two columns, hand-set feel. Headlines waiting on your witch names; the moment you christen them I'll write and lay out issue No. 1 for printing.$0
The citationOne broom at the rail wears a boot (foam clamp, painted iron-black) with a tag: “Per Hollow ordinance 7: overnight roosting. 2d fine.”$4
The lost cat gameHide a black cat statue somewhere new each night. Kids who spot her and report to the market get the good candy. The poster's already printed; the game costs nothing.$0
Cemetery dressingUntil the Sexton sheet gets built: two or three headstones from the kit (Sheet 6) and Rig C for the ground fog get the corner most of the way there this year.see S6
U6 · The Scattered Elements (fence, hats, scarecrows, birdhouses, benches)
~$40–60 total · scattered evenings · the connective tissue between the buildings
ElementUpgradeEst.
Pumpkin pail fence lineA flame tealight in every pail on the picket fence, all on one dusk timer. A row of grinning lanterns marking the village boundary at night, for about a dollar a pail.$12
The witch hats in the treesHang more at varying heights on fishing line so they sway, and tuck a warm micro fairy light up under each brim. After dark: floating hat lanterns, which reads as witches parked upstairs. This might be the best dollar-per-gasp upgrade in the yard.$15
Scarecrow familyThey're the seamstress's mannequins now (sign in U3). Give the child a tiny broom with a “LEARNER” tag from Bristle & Twig, and perch a crow on the parent's arm. Cross-references, everywhere, always.$5
BirdhousesRepaint as official Owl Post infrastructure: dark timber tones, a tiny “RAVEN ROOST No. 3” plate on each, one with a micro lit porthole. Your existing birdhouses become government buildings.$6
Hay bales & pumpkin clustersRegroup in odd numbers at building corners rather than lines, and hide three or four felt mice among them: more familiars for the hunt, and free composition.$8
The benchesOne gets a brass-look placard: “Reserved for elders of the coven.” Set a lantern beside the other and angle it toward the best sightline: you've just built the photo spot, and visitors will find it by themselves.$8
The burlap runnerEdge it with cut-branch borders and the path lanterns from the ideas list. A bordered path reads intentional; an unbordered one reads like a rug on grass.$0 + gathering
U7 · The House Problem (don't hide it, cast it)
~$50–80 · two evenings · the backdrop becomes a resident

The honest math first: a full-scale brick house cannot be hidden behind a 3/4-scale village, and draping it would cost more than three new builds. Hobbiton had the same problem with its hill and solved it the way theaters do: you don't hide the backdrop, you cast it. Three tools, in order of cost.

ToolHowEst.
Darkness (free)Never light the brick. Porch light off or swapped to the dimmest amber flame bulb you can buy, every village uplight angled away from the house, interior lights off in front rooms except as staged below. At night the eye goes where the light is, and the house simply recedes. This alone solves half the problem.$0
Screens (cheap)Fill the eye-level gaps between buildings, because that's where brick leaks through: corn-stalk screens (you already stage corn), lattice panels wearing creeper and your existing webbing, and dark burlap swags strung building-to-building like market rigging. For the gaps behind the commons: matte-black roofline flats (the distant-cottage technique, used as a background row), so between the real buildings visitors see more village silhouette instead of foundation brick.$30–50
Recruitment (the good one)The house joins the cast as the village's one grand building: the inn. Two or three visible front windows get removable leaded-pane film grids, amber glow, and one Rig A silhouette that passes occasionally upstairs. A hanging inn sign near the porch (“THE CROOKED KETTLE INN · no vacancies. ever.”), ivy swags softening the brick corners, a lantern and a pair of boots by the front door, and your porch becomes the inn's porch. Trick-or-treaters walking to your actual door are now walking into the inn, which means your candy handoff happens in character no matter where it happens.$25–40
Sequence matters: do darkness this week (it's free), screens as you place the new builds (their positions decide where the gaps are), and the inn dressing last, because once the windows glow amber with a moving shadow, visitors stop seeing a house at all. They see the biggest building in Coven Hollow, and the question “how do we hide the house” quietly retires itself.
U8 · Power, timers & the dusk switch
~$60–90 once · the sheet that makes the whole village run itself every night of October

Three GFCI-protected extension runs from your easy power, one per side of the yard, each ending in a weatherproof power strip inside a cord-safe box. Everything plugs into one of three zones, and the village wakes at dusk without you touching a thing.

ZoneFeedsControl
West (driveway side)Apothecary window + tower UV + bubbler, cemetery fog chiller, tiny-door micro lightsPhotocell dusk timer; fog on its own cycle timer
Center (commons)Cauldron stirrer + ember bed + mist, well light + mist, board lantern, path lanterns, audioPhotocell dusk timer; motors off at 10pm via a second timer if you like the village to “go to sleep”
East (market side)Market smoke + spinner + lantern, seamstress window + laundry fan, bench lightsPhotocell dusk timer; smoke on its cycle timer
  • Cords cross the walking path nowhere. Where a cord must cross grass kids run on, it goes under a rubber cable cover dressed with leaves.
  • Every fog machine lives in a vented weather box; every connection is up off the grass in a cord-safe box (dollar-store food containers with two notches work).
  • Buy one spare flame bulb, one spare fuse, and one spare fog timer in September. Something fails on October 30th every year, everywhere, always.

The Prop Shop

The prop master's mindset, in three rules. First: silhouette before detail. A prop reads from ten feet by its shape and value contrast, so get the outline and the darks right before fussing anything small. Second: everything ages. Nothing in Coven Hollow left the factory this decade, so every prop gets a wash, a dry-brush, or dust before it goes outside. Third: story beats craft. A mediocre loaf sitting in a bread queue ticket line tells more than a perfect loaf alone. Your spray-foam bread tutorial is exactly this school of thinking, and it's now canon below.
Recipe cards · food & market goods
RecipeMakesMethod
The bread loaves (your find, now canon)Loaves, rolls, buns for bakery + market, by the dozenSpray foam into dollar-store loaf tins and muffin tins, let cure proud of the rim, trim with a bread knife, seal with Mod Podge, paint with coffee-infused browns, dust cinnamon into the wet topcoat for crust texture. Batch 20 in a weekend. Matte-seal for outdoors.
PiesWindow pies, sill pies, feast piesDisc of floral foam or stacked cardboard in a real thrifted pie tin, dome it with spray foam or paper mache, paint crust colors, glossy Mod Podge tinted red or purple “filling” oozing at the edge, hot-glue lattice strips painted gold-brown. The gloss against matte crust is what sells it.
Market produce, the weird kindDragon eggs, screaming beets, odd gourdsPlastic easter eggs + tissue paper + Mod Podge = scaled dragon eggs (paint verdigris). Thrifted plastic produce gets a dark wash so it stops shining like plastic. Real gourds from your vines need nothing, which is the joke of faking everything else.
The feastInn Terrace table foodFoam roast (carved stiff floral foam, painted, gloss glaze), paper mache drumsticks, real bread props from the batch above, grapes are the one thing to buy fake because they read instantly. Half-eat everything with a knife before painting; abandoned mid-meal is the brief.
Cheese wheelsMarket + feast stacking goodsPool noodle coils or foam discs wrapped in muslin, painted wax-yellow, one wedge cut out and laid beside, red wax rind version = paint + glossy seal.
Recipe cards · aging, finishes & weathering
RecipeMakesMethod
The cinnamon rust (sister trick to your bread crust)Rusty hinges, brackets, lantern parts, the Sexton's toolsBrush watered white glue or dark brown paint where rust would collect (joints, low edges), sprinkle cinnamon into it wet, then dry-brush burnt orange and raw sienna over the texture once dry. Cheap hardware turns Victorian in ten minutes.
Coffee & tea paper agingEvery label, letter, poster, ledger page, Courier issuePrint, bathe in strong coffee or tea 5 minutes, crumple gently, uncrumple, bake at 200°F on a sheet pan until crisp, singe edges over a candle (outside, with water nearby). Batch a whole village's paperwork in one evening.
Wax seals without a kitSealed letters for the Owl Post by the bundleHot glue blob on the flap, press with a greased coat button or old coin, dry-brush deep red. A crayon melted into the glue stick tints the whole blob.
Crackle agePainted signs and shutters that look 80 years oldBase coat, dry. Brush plain school glue on, and while the glue is tacky paint the top coat over it. The top coat crackles as it dries, showing base color through. Dark wash after to pop the cracks.
Verdigris“Aged copper” on anything brass or gold-paintedTeal + mint acrylic stippled into recesses and drips, wiped off high spots. The C·H pillar box cipher, lantern tops, and the Diviner's moon dial all want this.
Instant dustApothecary shelves, book stacks, anywhere “undisturbed”Matte spray the prop, then sift gray pastel-chalk shavings (not cocoa or flour, which invite pests and rain-paste) onto it while tacky. Finger-swipe one clean streak: someone touched it recently. That streak is the storytelling.
Recipe cards · light, glass & the apothecary bench
RecipeMakesMethod
PVC drip candlesChandeliers, window candles, feast candelabra, by the dozenPVC pipe offcuts at varied heights, hot glue run down the sides in drips, painted bone or beeswax color, LED tealight in a countersunk top hole. Group in odd numbers on a base board. The single most-used prop in any haunt shop.
Potion bottlesApothecary stock, allotment dressing, market shelfThrifted glass + aged labels + corks dipped in crayon-tinted hot glue “wax.” Fill with colored water + glycerin (slows bubbles), layer sand or dried herbs as sediment. Tonic water in a few for the UV corner. Cluster odd numbers, vary heights.
Specimen jarsThe curiosities shelf (very Memento Mori)Dollar-store creatures (snakes, frogs) in tea-tinted water, lid rusted with the cinnamon trick, label in Latin-ish: “Ranae · do not release.” One jar lying on its side, empty, lid off: something got out.
Lantern conversionsEvery lantern in the villageAny thrifted lantern + flame-flicker LED bulb or fairy-light bundle + amber film if the glass is clear. Never white light. Batch-convert on one bench day.
The Smoke Program (chimneys that breathe, the Hobbiton dream)
Two rigs: an automated every-night system, and an attended special-occasion system for your church incense. Plus the one trick that makes either visible: light.

Rule zero, and it's absolute: nothing burns in, on, or against a foam chimney, ever. Foam ignites fast, drips while burning, and the fumes are genuinely toxic. Your instinct to stop was the correct prop-master instinct. Combustion lives in metal, on the ground, at a distance; the chimney is only ever a decorative smokestack that borrowed smoke rises through.

The Chimney Rule, now village law: every future chimney is designed smoke-ready from the first sketch. Hollow core for the duct, ground space at the base for the machine, cord path to a power zone, restricted exit at the crown. Current chimney census: the bakery (rigged in its packet), Coven Market's pair (rig in Upgrade Sheet U2), Bristle & Twig's stove pipe (same rig, smaller duct), and the apothecary's stone chimney (a candidate for a third rig once the first two prove out). The far cottage's chimney stays painted-on; a silhouette that smokes would draw the eye to what should stay unseen.

Rig 1. The every-night smoke (fog machine, automated)

PartSpec
MachineSmall 400W fogger in a vented weather box on the ground behind the building. Small is correct: a 1000W machine reads as a house fire.
JuiceThis is the visibility secret most people miss. Standard juice vanishes in seconds; long hang-time formulas (Froggy's Swamp Juice or any “long-lasting / high-density” blend) produce wisps that linger and curl like real woodsmoke.
Delivery4″ duct from the nozzle up the inside of the chimney. Restrict the top exit to a 2–3″ opening: the narrower mouth turns a cloud into a rising ribbon. An 80mm PC fan just below the exit gives it a steady lazy push.
TimingCycle timer: about 10 seconds of puff, 60–90 of rest on calm nights. On canyon-breeze nights, shorten to 5-second puffs more often; small frequent wisps survive wind that shreds long blasts.
Two chimneys, one machineThe Coven Market's pair of pots can share one fogger through a Y-splitter in the duct, offset so the pots don't puff in unison. Houses breathe unevenly.

Rig 2. The censer rig (your church incense, attended nights only)

Hobbiton's incense smoke is finer than fog, hangs beautifully, and smells like a holy place, which is why you remember it. It can be done safely, but treat it like operating a tiny wood stove, not like a decoration.

PartSpec
The fireboxA cast-iron dutch oven, small kettle grill, or steel chafing pan on the ground, set on pavers or cinder blocks, positioned behind the building 12″+ clear of any foam or straw. Self-lighting charcoal tablet inside, resin incense spooned on top: this is exactly how a church censer works.
The flueRigid metal duct or stovepipe (never vinyl dryer hose, which is plastic) rising from a metal hood over the firebox up through the chimney's hollow core. The metal pipe extends 2″ above the foam cap, so warm smoke exits without ever touching foam, and keep 3″ of air gap between pipe and foam the whole way up. Heat does the lifting; no fan needed.
The screenA dome of metal window-screen mesh over the pipe top. Charcoal tablets rarely spark, and the screen makes rarely into never.
The rulesAttended, always: this rig runs only while you're outside with it, on calm nights, with a fire extinguisher and a water bucket staged. It's the Halloween-night and party-night effect; Rig 1 handles the other thirty nights of October on a timer.
The bonusIncense is also your smell layer for the whole street. One censer night will out-perform every scent trick in the ideas list.

The visibility trick that outranks both rigs

Hobbiton's smoke read because it was photographed against daylight. At night, smoke is invisible until light touches it, so the real secret is a small amber spotlight hidden behind or below each chimney top, grazing upward through the exit. Lit from behind, even a thin wisp glows like a living thing; unlit, the best smoke in the world reads as nothing. Aim the beam so it catches the smoke and not the foam, test on the first calm night, and expect neighbors to slow their cars.

Recipe cards · structure skins, stone & growth
RecipeMakesMethod
Monster mudRigid draped fabric, stone skins, the well's rock coatThe haunt-industry classic: 1 part exterior latex paint to 4-5 parts joint compound. Dip burlap or old sheets and drape (they dry rigid), or trowel over foam for instant aged plaster and stone. Paint when cured.
Foam wood grainEvery plank surface in the villageScore planks with a ballpoint, drag a wire brush lengthwise for grain, poke knots with a pencil. Black or umber base, gray dry-brush, cream dry-brush catching only the ridges, dark wash into the scores. Your Coven Market proves you already own this skill.
Tombstone schoolShady Willow's expansionThis is VanOaks Props territory: 2″ foam, hot-knife lettering, layered stone paint (base, wash, two dry-brushes), edges beaten with a chain and wire brush before painting. Their tutorials go deep on the paint layering that makes foam read as granite; worth an evening of watching before you carve.
Moss, three speedsRoof edges, north faces, stone shouldersFast: preserved sheet moss glued with construction adhesive. Faster: flock or sawdust dyed green, sprinkled onto tacky paint. Fanciest: mix both, moss in the crevices and flock feathering out. Keep it to north faces and drip lines; moss everywhere reads fake, moss where water would sit reads old.
Cobwebs that read realCorners of every structureSkip spray webs. Pull apart cotton batting into wisps and stretch until nearly transparent, catch on two points, let the middle sag. Dust lightly gray. Webs sag with age; taut webs read as store-bought.
Channels, shops & products (the time-savers)
SourceWhat it's for
VanOaks Props (YouTube + vanoaksprops.com + Patreon)The tombstone and paint-aging school. Their layered paint tutorials are the difference between foam that looks like foam and foam that looks like hundred-year-old granite. Watch before the Shady Willow expansion.
Memento Mori Curiosities & Props (YouTube + mementomoriprops.com)Curiosities, potion and specimen aesthetics, exactly your apothecary's world. Study their finishes for the shelf tower and the specimen jars.
Monster City StudiosThe big-league sculpted statement props (theme-park tier). Treat as inspiration and as the someday-splurge shelf; one anchor piece from this tier can headline a zone.
The Horror Dome / HauntedProps.com / HauntWorld's supplier directoryPro haunt vendors for the things not worth building: quality ravens and owls, animatronics if you ever want one, static creatures. HauntWorld's directory is the index of the whole industry.
Froggy's FogFog juice by behavior: low-lying formulas for the cemetery crawl, scented juice (campfire, fall spice) for the fire pit. Better juice matters more than a better machine.
AtmosFXDigital window projections: the professional big sibling of the mirror-ball shadow spinner. One projector + their witch silhouette loops in an upstairs Inn window is a splurge that carries the whole house recruitment plan.
Dollar stores, restatedNot a decor source, a raw-materials supplier: loaf tins, lanterns for conversion, glassware, tealights, foam boards, cheesecloth. Walk it with prop-master eyes: never ask “is this spooky,” ask “what is this shaped like.”
The production calendar (a prop shop runs all year)
SeasonShop focus
NovStrike + post-mortem: photograph everything before teardown, note what failed in weather, buy clearance (lanterns, fog machines, crows go 50–70% off Nov 1). Write next year's wish list while it's fresh.
Dec–FebBench season, indoors: bread batches, pies, candles, potion bottles, wax-sealed letters, all paper props, name plates, signs lettered at the kitchen table. Small, warm, batchable work. This is where your head start lives.
Mar–MayAntique season (your shops restock from estate sales) + the paint shop: age and finish everything built over winter, cinnamon-rust the hardware, convert lanterns.
Jun–JulGarage framing season: wall panels, roofs, the big builds, painted flat on sawhorses in good weather. Vines get trained on the arches.
AugAssembly tests: pin-hinge fit, rig bench-tests (fog, spinners, stirrer, timers), one full mock-up of the hardest build in the driveway.
SepFinish work: moss, shingles, signage hung, headstones planted, zones laid out with stakes and string per the map.
OctInstall in layers (structures week 1, rigs week 2, dressing week 3, kill-list fixes week 4), and the village wakes at dusk on its timers all month.
Bench rules: batch identical props (twelve loaves take barely longer than three), seal everything matte for weather, test one prop of each type through a sprinkler night before trusting the design, and keep a “hero table” where each finished prop sits a week where you'll walk past it. If it still delights you after seven passes, it earns a spot in the village.
